events.headline: India cuts import duty on palm, soybean oils to lower edible oil prices

items.title: India cuts import duty on palm, soybean oils to lower edible oil prices
items.summary: The move comes amid rising food inflation and industry concerns over global vegetable oil supplies, domestic availability and festive-season demand

items.title: Centre asks edible oil firms to pass duty-cut benefits on to consumers
items.summary: The directive follows cuts in import duties on sunflower, soybean and palm oils as the government seeks to moderate domestic prices and ease inflationary pressures

events.article_text:
The government has cut import duty on sunflower, soybean and palm oils from September 24 as refined oil inflation rises and edible oil imports increase.

The government has cut import duty on crude and refined sunflower, soybean, and palm oil to reduce edible oil prices in the domestic market. The duty cuts will be effective from September 24.

The basic customs duty (BCD) on crude Soybean Oil and Palm Oil has been slashed from 10 per cent to 5 per cent, and on refined Soybean Oil and Palm Oil from 32.5 per cent to 27.5 per cent. Meanwhile, the BCD on crude Sunflower Oil has been abolished; previously, it was 10 per cent. But import duty on refined Sunflower Oil has been trimmed to 22.5 per cent from 32.5 per cent, the finance ministry said in a notification.

The All India Consumer Food Price Index (CFPI) for August was 5.95 per cent, up from 5.52 per cent in July. In the food basket, retail inflation in refined oil, the most consumed edible oil, has been rising steadily since moving to double digits (10.25 per cent) in April from 7.62 per cent in March, and in August it recorded 14.24 per cent.

Sudhakar Desai, President of the Indian Vegetable Oil Producers’ Association (IVPA), said the decision comes at an important juncture, particularly with the festive season approaching. At the consumer level, however, the impact of any duty reduction will depend on several factors beyond customs duties, including international commodity prices, freight costs, exchange-rate movements, domestic availability and inventory levels, he said.

Stating that lower import duties should improve the landed costs of imported edible oils, which can provide some reduction in consumer prices, Desai said the immediate priority for the sector is to ensure adequate availability across the country during the upcoming festival months, with higher household demand as well as increased requirements from the sweets, snacks, food-service and HORECA segments.

“Industry especially in north and north east has been reeling under the pressure of zero duty imports from Nepal due to duty arbitrage with Indian duties which will continue as Nepal goods will still be more competitive compared to domestically refined oils. IVPA has been demanding an import quota on zero duty imports from SAFTA countries,” he added.

The Solvent Extractors’ Association of India (SEA) highlighted potential volatility in the global edible oil sector during its recent meeting with senior government officials on September 21. In his monthly letter to the members, SEA President Sanjeev Asthana said that the government was apprised of the current edible oil stocks and supply situation.

Stating that the industry flagged potential volatility ahead, he said the possible impact of El Niño, continued uncertainty around sunflower oil supplies amid the Russia-Ukraine conflict and Indonesia’s B50 biodiesel programme could alter the global vegetable oil balance. This could increase the strategic importance of soybean and soybean oil in the coming months, he added.

India’s edible oil imports grew 4.56 per cent during the first 10 months of the oil year 2025-26 (November-October), driven by an increase in imports of palm oil and soybean oil.

Data compiled by SEA showed that India imported 136.19 lakh tonnes (lt) of edible oil during November-August of the oil year 2025-26, up from 130.24 lt in the corresponding period of 2024-25.

Palm oil imports (including crude palm oil and RBD palmolein) increased to 65.34 lt during the first 10 months of the oil year 2025-26 from 61.47 lt in the corresponding period of the previous oil year. During the period, soybean oil imports increased to 45.61 lt (from 44.64 lt) and sunflower oil imports to 25.15 lt (from 24 lt).

analysis.tldr: The government is slashing import taxes on cooking oils, which should help lower grocery bills for households as the festive season approaches.
the_story: The government cut import taxes on sunflower, soybean, and palm oils starting September 24 to lower domestic cooking oil prices.
The basic customs duty on crude soybean and palm oils dropped from 10% to 5%, while crude sunflower oil duty was completely removed.
Retail inflation (rate of price rise) for refined oil hit 14.24% in August, prompting the government to act as imports rose to 136.19 lakh tonnes.
Industry experts warn that global factors like El Niño, the Russia-Ukraine conflict, and Indonesia's biodiesel program could still cause price volatility.
analysis.what_happened: The Indian government reduced import taxes (basic customs duties) on crude and refined edible oils like palm, soybean, and sunflower. This decision was triggered by a steady rise in retail cooking oil inflation—which climbed to 14.24% in August—and growing edible oil imports.
analysis.analogy: It is like a grocery shop owner lowering the wholesale tax they pay on imported cooking oil, hoping the lower cost makes bottles cheaper for families buying for a festival feast.
why_it_matters_india: Government cuts import taxes on edible oils ->
It becomes cheaper for traders to bring in palm, soybean, and sunflower oil from abroad ->
The Centre asks edible oil companies to pass these savings on to everyday buyers ->
Household grocery expenses for cooking oil drop, easing the burden of food inflation on families.

impacts.rationale: Cheaper cooking oil imports reduce food inflation, which is good for household budgets.

impacts.target: FMCG (Fast-Moving Consumer Goods) stocks like Marico or Adani Wilmar
impacts.rationale: Lower raw material costs can improve profit margins for edible oil and food processing companies.

watch_next: Whether edible oil companies actually lower retail prices on store shelves
Global weather patterns like El Niño and supplies from Ukraine and Indonesia
analysis.caveats: If international commodity prices or shipping freight costs jump sharply overseas, the tax cut might not translate into lower prices at local stores.

events.headline: After Moody's, now S&P and Fitch raise their India growth forecasts

items.title: After Moody's, now S&P and Fitch raise their India growth forecasts
items.summary: Both rating agencies see an interest rate hike coming this fiscal year on high inflation, strong growth and the war in West Asia.

events.article_text:
A number of global agencies raised their growth forecasts for India in the range of 40 to 80 basis points (bps) for the fiscal year through March 2027, citing the country’s resilience amid the West Asia war and higher-than-expected 7.8% expansion in the June quarter.

They, however, projected growth to moderate in the second half of the fiscal year from the June quarter level, with at least two of them—global rating agencies S&P and Fitch—expecting inflationary pressure to mount in the wake of the conflict and below-par monsoon rains.

This could lead the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to raise the interest rates, they said in separate statements.

Still, the projected growth rates keep India as the fastest-growing major economy amid the global turmoil.

While S&P has revised up its FY27 India growth forecast to 7% from the previously-reported 6.6%, Fitch has raised it to 6.9% from 6.4%, both joining their peer Moody's, which raised its projection last week to 7% from 6%.

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) on Wednesday raised its FY27 India growth forecast to 7.1% from 6.3%. It said growth was underpinned by resilient domestic demand and government policies that cushioned households and companies from the impact of higher energy prices.

The Asian Development Bank (ADB), too, raised its forecast for the country to 7% from 6.6%. “Despite supply disruptions and high commodity prices, India’s economy continues to demonstrate resilience, supported by strong infrastructure spending and growth-supporting fiscal and monetary policies,” ADB country director for India Mio Oka said in a statement.

Continued strength in services, including AI-related investments, alongside improvements in farm productivity and steady manufacturing growth, will help sustain the growth momentum, Oka added.

The multilateral lender, however, cut its growth forecast for the next fiscal year marginally to 7.1% from 7.3%.

OECD said, “Despite recent strong momentum, reduced purchasing power is also expected to weaken growth in India through the second half of this year, before a gradual recovery takes place in 2027.” It predicted growth to slow down to 6.5% in FY28.

S&P, too, expected a moderation in growth momentum, going forward. "(We) expect growth to ease in the second half of the fiscal year as the tailwinds from general sales tax (goods and services tax) rationalization and income tax cuts diminish. Weather-related risks warrant close monitoring," S&P said.

Cumulative rains were 15% below normal until 9 September in the current monsoon season, S&P said, adding farm output and food inflation remain key variables to watch.

Fitch expects growth to moderate over the rest of the financial year. It cited a slower pace of expansion in both manufacturing and services in the purchasing managers' index, impact of below-normal monsoon rains on growth in farm and rural demand and rising inflation that, it said, will constrain real incomes and consumer dynamics.

However, it expected private investment prospects to look more buoyant, projecting a more than 10% rise this fiscal year. As for FY28, Fitch projected growth to settle at 6.5%, as the energy price shock unwinds, with consumer spending and investment driving growth. It expects growth to touch 6.5% in FY29 as well.

S&P expects the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to raise the interest rate by 25 basis points this fiscal to 5.5%, flagging persistent inflationary pressures in times of high growth, an unresolved conflict in West Asia, and weather-related risks. Fitch reckons the RBI could raise the interest rate by 25 basis points in the next monetary policy committee meeting in October and by another 25 basis points in early 2027, "given the combination of strong demand, price rises, and adverse supply developments". Fitch said the interest rates could then ease back to 5.5% in 2028.

"We expect the balance of considerations to shift toward higher interest rates. Factors supporting this shift include solid growth, persistent inflationary pressures, an unresolved conflict in West Asia, and weather-related risks," S&P said, forecasting a 25 bps hike in the interest rate in FY27.

The biggest rating agency expected consumer price inflation to average 5.1% in FY27, a tad higher than RBI's 5% forecast.

Fitch expected retail inflation to increase in the short term, touching 5.5% in December this year from 4.82% in August, before easing. It also expected the rupee to remain close to current levels against the dollar for the rest of the year, and to depreciate slightly next year.

analysis.tldr: Major global agencies have upgraded India's growth forecasts, but warn that rising inflation and possible interest rate hikes could soon make loans more expensive for ordinary people.
the_story: Global agencies including S&P, Fitch, Moody's, OECD, and the Asian Development Bank raised India's growth forecasts for the fiscal year through March 2027 by 40 to 80 basis points (bps [hundredths of a percent]), keeping India the fastest-growing major economy.
OECD raised its forecast to 7.1% from 6.3%, while S&P and ADB raised theirs to 7%, and Fitch increased its projection to 6.9%.
Agencies cited a strong 7.8% expansion in the June quarter, solid domestic demand, government infrastructure spending, and services growth as key drivers.

However, S&P and Fitch warned that growth will moderate later in the year due to below-par monsoon rains (cumulative rains were 15% below normal by September 9), rising inflation, and West Asia war tensions.
S&P and Fitch expect the Reserve Bank of India (RBI [India's central bank that controls interest rates and money supply]) to raise interest rates by 25 to 50 basis points to fight climbing prices.
analysis.what_happened: Major international rating agencies raised India's economic growth predictions because the country expanded by a stronger-than-expected 7.8% in the June quarter. Even so, these agencies caution that poor monsoon rains and conflicts in West Asia will push prices up, likely forcing the Reserve Bank of India to hike interest rates.
analysis.analogy: It is like a car driving at top speed on a highway, but the driver notices fuel running low and a rough patch ahead, meaning they must step on the brakes a little bit.
why_it_matters_india: Global agencies boost India's growth outlook, showing strong domestic demand and infrastructure spending.
Below-normal monsoon rains and West Asia war pressures threaten to increase food and energy inflation.
Rising inflation prompts global agencies to predict that the RBI will increase borrowing costs.
Higher interest rates make loans costlier for everyday consumers while potentially cooling down spending.

impacts.target: Interest rates on loans (home, car, and personal loans)
impacts.rationale: If the RBI raises its benchmark interest rate to fight inflation, banks will pass those costs on, making EMIs [equated monthly installments - fixed monthly loan payments] more expensive for borrowers.
Poor monsoon rains and supply disruptions from West Asia are expected to push retail inflation higher in the short term, which reduces household purchasing power — bad for everyday consumers.
Fitch expects the rupee to depreciate (lose value against the dollar) slightly next year, which makes imported goods like crude oil more expensive for India.

watch_next: The Reserve Bank of India's upcoming monetary policy committee meetings for any announcements on interest rate hikes.
Retail inflation data and food price movements following below-normal monsoon rains.
analysis.caveats: Growth could turn out differently if weather conditions improve unexpectedly or global commodity prices shift rapidly.

events.article_text:
Russia Begins Oil Exports From Its Giant Vostok Arctic Project

Julianne Geiger is a veteran energy journalist and market analyst with more than a decade of experience covering the global oil and gas sector. Her…

Russia has begun commercial crude exports from Rosneft’s Vostok Oil project, putting barrels on the water from its new Arctic terminal after years of sanctions, investor exits, and construction delays.

Three ice-class tankers loaded about 250,000 metric tons of crude from the Bukhta Sever terminal on the Taimyr Peninsula in September. Two carried the oil to Murmansk for ship-to-ship transfer. A third headed for Asia through the Northern Sea Route. A fourth tanker is waiting to load.

Industry sources expect exports to average about 150,000 barrels per day this year, equal to just 7.5% of the 2 million bpd once envisioned for Vostok.

Much of that initial supply is coming from Rosneft’s mature Vankor fields. Rosneft says development of northern fields, including Payakha, could lift exports to around 600,000 bpd in the second half of 2027 and 1 million bpd by 2030.

Vostok covers 13 fields holding an estimated 50 billion barrels of low-sulfur crude. A dedicated 790-kilometer pipeline connects the development to Bukhta Sever, where Rosneft plans a 100-tank storage hub.

Trafigura and Vitol pulled out of Vostok after Western sanctions were imposed on Russia in 2022, taking two major international investors with them. Rosneft had to replace that money with domestic financing and asset sales, and commercial exports slipped years behind schedule.

Those barrels are entering a market where one of Russia’s biggest customers is already buying less. India cut Russian crude imports 16.5% in August to about 2.1 million bpd, and preliminary Kpler data puts September at 1.9 million bpd. A new U.S. sanctions law provides for tariffs of up to 100% on goods from major buyers of Russian oil and gas.

Russia produced about 9.9 million bpd of oil and condensate in 2025, compared with nearly 13.6 million bpd in the United States.

Bukhta Sever gives those new barrels an Arctic export path as well. One of the first commercial cargoes is already sailing east through the Northern Sea Route, away from Russia’s Baltic and Black Sea oil infrastructure that has been hit by Ukrainian drone attacks.

the_story: Russia started commercial crude exports from its Rosneft Vostok Oil project in the Arctic, shipping oil from the Bukhta Sever terminal on the Taimyr Peninsula in September.
Three ice-class tankers loaded about 250,000 metric tons of crude in September, with exports expected to average 150,000 barrels per day this year.
International investors like Trafigura and Vitol pulled out after Western sanctions in 2022, forcing Rosneft to use domestic financing and delay the project.

analysis.what_happened: Russia has finally launched oil exports from its massive Vostok project in the Arctic after years of delays and foreign investors walking away due to Western sanctions. To get this oil moving, Russia had to rely on domestic funding instead of foreign money. These new barrels are entering the global market just as one of its biggest buyers, India, is slowing down its purchases.
analysis.analogy: It is like a factory opening a new production line after a difficult delay, but finding that its biggest regular customer is currently shopping around less.
why_it_matters_india: Russia starts exporting new Arctic oil -> global oil supply increases
At the same time, India cuts its Russian oil imports (down to 1.9 million barrels per day in September) -> India looks for alternative energy sources
New U.S. sanctions threaten high tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil -> Indian refiners tread more carefully to avoid trade penalties
More global oil supply meeting steady demand -> helps keep international crude prices stable, which supports stable domestic fuel costs in India

impacts.rationale: Extra oil supply coming from Russia's new Arctic project can put downward pressure on global prices, which is good for import-dependent nations like India.
Cheaper or stable global crude oil eventually helps ease fuel costs at home, which is good for household budgets.

watch_next: Whether India continues to lower its imports of Russian crude oil in the coming months
How strictly the new U.S. sanctions law regarding buyers of Russian energy is enforced
analysis.caveats: Geopolitical tensions or stricter enforcement of sanctions could quickly disrupt these new Arctic shipping routes.

analysis.tldr: If the rupee strengthens, imported things like crude oil and electronics could become slightly cheaper for ordinary people.
the_story: RBI (Reserve Bank of India, India's central bank) Deputy Governor Poonam Gupta stated that the rupee (Indian currency) could stabilize or appreciate (gain value against other currencies) following its recent depreciation (loss in value).

She pointed out India's ability to lower the current account deficit (the gap between money going out and coming into the country) using services exports and remittances (money sent home by Indians working abroad).
Gupta stated that capital account (records of international money flows) conditions could improve, which would help boost foreign investments.
She also highlighted that the RBI has the capacity to handle external pressures and keep exchange rates orderly.
analysis.what_happened: RBI Deputy Governor Poonam Gupta publicly expressed a positive outlook for the Indian rupee, suggesting it might gain strength rather than just steady itself. This view is driven by expectations that India's strong services exports, incoming money from abroad, and improving conditions for foreign investments will support the domestic currency.
analysis.analogy: It is like a household whose members are suddenly sending home much more money from their jobs abroad, making the family's piggy bank feel heavier and more confident against outside expenses.
why_it_matters_india: The RBI official indicates that India's incoming money from services and remittances will stay strong -> this brings more foreign currency into the country.
More foreign currency entering India boosts the value of the rupee -> making the rupee appreciate or stabilize.
A stronger rupee lowers the cost of importing goods like crude oil -> which helps reduce domestic inflationary pressures (rising prices).
Better capital conditions encourage foreign investors -> supporting India's overall financial stability.

impacts.rationale: Stronger export and investment outlooks could help the currency gain value, which is generally good because it makes imports cheaper for consumers.
A stronger rupee reduces the cost of imported goods like oil, helping keep everyday price rises under control for ordinary people.

watch_next: Actual monthly data on India's current account deficit and services exports
Trends in foreign investments flowing into the country
analysis.caveats: Global economic shocks or unexpected shifts in international markets could change the path of the currency.

events.headline: Seoul Needs a Playbook for Hormuz, Ukraine, and What Comes Next

items.title: Seoul Needs a Playbook for Hormuz, Ukraine, and What Comes Next
items.summary: Earlier this month, President Donald Trump shared a Washington Post opinion piece on his social media, arguing that South Korea should send its Cheongung-II air-defense system to Ukraine. Additionally, the Trump administration continues to pressure Seoul to send troops to the Strait of Hormuz. Neither the U.S.-Iranian conflict nor the Russo-Ukrainian War is new, yet the simultaneity of U.S. pressure on Seoul to help in its war with Iran and to support Ukraine is striking.While such diverging asks are indeed unprecedented, this is partly due to a lack of principles that stipulate a clear South

events.article_text:
While such diverging asks are indeed unprecedented, this is partly due to a lack of principles that stipulate a clear South Korean position. South Korea should establish a principle that requires multilateral legitimacy before it deploys its own troops overseas. It should also build a Lend-Lease-style legal framework, modeled on the World War II-era law, to govern arms sales to partners like Ukraine. In the absence of such principles, Seoul will continue to scramble each time an ally or partner calls, ultimately signaling its unpredictability and unreliability. As a member of the National Assembly who would cast one of the votes on any Hormuz deployment, I may soon be asked to vote for a decision Seoul is making without ever having settled the principle that should govern it.

A potential troop deployment to the Strait of Hormuz is complicated by independent equities Seoul holds in Iran. Seoul and Tehran built cultural ties dating to a 1969 Treaty of Friendship and a 1977 street-naming exchange, and economic ties that once sent more than 200,000 South Koreans to work in Iran’s infrastructure sector. As recently as 2017, Iran supplied 13.2 percent of South Korea’s oil imports, its third-largest source. That relationship still carries financial weight: From 2018 until 2023, South Korea held roughly $6 billion in frozen Iranian oil revenue, released only as part of a separate U.S.-Iranian prisoner swap.

Beijing and Moscow have stakes in these conflicts that far exceed Seoul’s own. China buys as much as 90 percent of Iran’s oil exports, making it far more exposed to any disruption in the Strait of Hormuz than South Korea is. China, South Korea’s largest trading partner, has also used economic retaliation in response to Seoul’s deployment of Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, a history that Seoul cannot ignore. Furthermore, Russia has issued a comparable warning directly to Seoul. When Seoul considered joining a NATO-led initiative to help purchase U.S. weapons for Ukraine, the Russian foreign ministry threatened “retaliatory measures, including ‘asymmetric’ ones.” Both powers have more at stake in these conflicts and more capacity to retaliate than South Korea does.

In the past, Seoul has deployed its troops to assist its ally, the United States, as well as in support of United Nations missions. For instance, Seoul sent roughly 320,000 troops to Vietnam, the largest foreign contingent after the United States, at the request of the United States. South Korea also deployed the Zaytun Division to Iraq from 2004 to 2008 as the third-largest contingent. Seoul also maintained the Akh unit in the Emirates, Dongmyeong with the U.N. force in Lebanon, and Hanbit in South Sudan. The record reflects a mixture of alliance assistance, non-combat roles when possible, and adherence to the National Assembly’s consent requirement. Nevertheless, Seoul needs a codified principle to govern its overseas troop deployment going forward.

Case in point: Seoul is having a premature public discussion of troop deployment only a few weeks after its annual joint military exercise with the United States was abruptly canceled and downsized. Are joint military operations fit for purpose when the very exercise meant to prepare that posture has just been cut? As Seoul’s internal debate over potential troop deployment is reported in the media, and the Defense Ministry confirmed it has sent a survey team to the Strait to assess conditions, the South Korean public is rightfully asking the same question. The South Korean president’s office has since ordered an audit to identify which agency leaked the internal deliberation, confirming that its own process lacks the discipline a governing principle would impose.

What further complicates matters for both American and South Korean policymakers is that any overseas troop deployment requires the consent of the National Assembly. In April 2003, the National Assembly approved sending non-combat engineering and medical units to Iraq. The more consequential vote came in Feb. 2004. It approved a separate and far larger deployment, a roughly 3,000-troop Zaytun Division. Seoul structured Zaytun under its own independent command, designated primarily for peacekeeping. The unit is named “Zaytun,” Arabic for “olive,” as a symbol of peace. The deployment rested on U.N. Security Council resolutions 1511 and 1546 — legal backing that the current case for Iran lacks.

The first Trump administration’s crisis with Iran heightened in the aftermath of the Fujairah attacks, the Saudi Aramco strike, and the Qassem Soleimani killing. In response, Seoul chose to expand its forward-deployed Cheonghae unit into the Gulf of Oman and the Persian Gulf without joining the U.S.-proposed International Maritime Security Construct. It was a compromise made to assist the United States in protecting sea routes for shipping and energy imports and maintaining a long-term relationship with Iran. Yet, Seoul expanded the Cheonghae unit’s area of operation to bypass the National Assembly’s consent, drawing widespread criticism from lawmakers. It was based on a clause governing the Cheonghae unit’s deployment, which allows its operating area to expand to protect South Korean citizens during a crisis.

While the 2020 approach was an attempt to maintain ambiguity in complicated geopolitics, such an episode cannot be repeated during a hot war situation in the Strait of Hormuz today. Initial media coverage included, and the Ministry of Defense has yet to confirm, potential assets such as P-8A Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft, a naval explosive ordnance disposal team, and a logistics support ship, with missions running to surveillance to mine clearing. Even so, the government and ruling party admit that such a mission requires the National Assembly’s consent regardless of its non-combat nature. What further complicates matters is the ruling party’s ambivalence about the mission’s clarity and necessity, leaving it uncertain

analysis.tldr: Rising tensions in key oil shipping routes like the Strait of Hormuz could push up global crude oil prices, which directly increases fuel and inflation costs for India.
the_story: South Korea is debating whether to deploy troops and military assets, such as P-8A Poseidon aircraft and naval teams, to the Strait of Hormuz.
South Korea has historical ties with Iran, including past economic links where Iran supplied 13.2 percent of South Korean oil imports in 2017.
China buys up to 90 percent of Iran's oil exports and is South Korea's largest trading partner, making South Korea sensitive to potential economic retaliation from Beijing.
Any overseas troop deployment by South Korea requires formal consent from its National Assembly, which previously approved missions like the Zaytun Division in Iraq.
analysis.what_happened: South Korea is struggling to form a clear foreign policy framework on whether to deploy military support to global conflict zones like Ukraine and the Strait of Hormuz. Because it lacks clear standing principles, its internal discussions and leaked government plans are causing confusion while trying to balance ties with the U.S., China, and Iran.
analysis.analogy: It is like a household trying to decide whether to lend money or get involved in neighborhood disputes without having a clear family rulebook first, leading to loud arguments every time a neighbor asks for help.
why_it_matters_india: Geopolitical friction in oil-exporting regions like the Strait of Hormuz threatens global oil supply routes.
Any disruption or fear of supply shortages causes international crude oil prices to rise.
Because India imports a vast majority of its crude oil, pricier global oil increases the cost of importing fuel.
Higher import bills weaken the rupee (each rupee buys fewer dollars) and drive up domestic inflation (the rate at which prices rise).

impacts.rationale: Uncertainty and potential disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz can cause oil prices to spike, which is bad for consumers as it raises fuel costs.
Costlier oil imports mean India needs more dollars to buy energy, pushing the rupee down—generally bad for Indian purchasing power.
More expensive imported fuel filters through the economy, making goods and transport costlier for regular people.

watch_next: Official updates on South Korea's National Assembly decisions regarding troop deployment
Any actual disruptions to commercial shipping or oil flows in the Strait of Hormuz
analysis.caveats: This text focuses heavily on South Korea's internal political debate and legislation rather than an active military blockade, meaning actual market impacts depend heavily on whether a physical crisis in the oil shipping lanes actually materializes.

why_it_matters_india: High global oil prices mean India has to spend more dollars to buy crude oil from abroad.
When oil gets costly, it puts pressure on the overall economy and makes running businesses more expensive.
Investors get worried about higher costs eating into company profits, causing them to sell shares.
This selling pressure drags down major stock indices like the Nifty, especially affecting big sectors like banking.

events.headline: Russian Federation notifies launch of safeguard investigation on certain flat steel products

items.title: Russian Federation notifies launch of safeguard investigation on certain flat steel products
items.summary: On 9 September 2026, the Russian Federation notified the WTO’s Committee on Safeguards regarding the initiation on 7 September 2026 of a safeguard investigation on certain flat steel products with polymer coating imported into the customs territory of the Eurasian Economic Union.

events.article_text:
In the notification the Russian Federation indicated, among other things, as follows:

"4. Provide a point of contact for the investigation and identify the preferred means for corresponding.

The point of contact would be available to respond to enquiries relating to the procedures applicable to the investigation.

Department for Internal Market Defence (DIMD)

Tel +7 (495) 669-24-00 #4949,#4966,#3224,# 3097,#1316,# 4955,# 1272

5. Provide the deadlines and procedures for importers, exporters and other interested parties to present evidence and their views, including:

(i) deadlines and procedures for Members and exporters to identify themselves as interested parties, if so required, to participate in the investigation and (ii) the date of an intended public hearing as provided for in Article 3.1. Note: At the time of the initiation, if the authority has not decided whether or not to hold such a hearing, or if the date of the hearing is undetermined, Members should indicate under this item how such information would be publicized. Members are not obliged to submit another notification simply due to the fact that the proposed date has subsequently been changed.

In accordance with the Protocol on Application of Safeguard, Anti-Dumping and Countervailing Measures with respect to Third Countries (Annex No. 8 to the Treaty on the Eurasian Economic Union of 29 May 2014), interested parties may declare their intention to seek participant status not later than 25 days from the date of initiation of the investigation. Participants to the safeguard investigation have the right to request access to the non-confidential file and participate in public hearings.

The participants to the safeguard investigation may request for public hearings within 45 days from the date of initiation of the investigation.

Interested parties should submit comments within 60 days from the date of the initiation of the investigation in writing in the Russian language to the following address (for more details visit the following website: https://remedies.eaeunion.org/dimd/ru/security/investigations/card/SG-15):

The notification is available in G/SG/N/6/RUS/10.

A safeguard investigation seeks to determine whether increased imports of a product are causing, or are threatening to cause, serious injury to a domestic industry.

During a safeguard investigation, importers, exporters and other interested parties may present evidence and views and respond to the presentations of other parties.

A WTO member may take a safeguard action (i.e. restrict imports of a product temporarily) only if the increased imports of the product are found to be causing, or threatening to cause, serious injury.

Problems viewing this page? If so, please contact [email protected] giving details of the operating system and web browser you are using.

analysis.tldr: Russia is investigating steel imports to see if they hurt local factories, which could block foreign steel and change where global metal flows.
the_story: The Russian Federation notified the World Trade Organization (WTO [an international group that sets global trade rules]) that it has launched a safeguard investigation on certain flat steel products.
The investigation is being handled by Russia's Department for Internal Market Defence (DIMD).
Interested parties have 25 days to declare participant status, 45 days to request public hearings, and 60 days to submit written comments in the Russian language.
A safeguard investigation checks whether rising imports are harming local industries, which can lead to temporary restrictions on foreign goods if harm is found.
analysis.what_happened: Russia officially informed the World Trade Organization that it is starting a safeguard investigation into flat steel imports. This type of investigation happens when a country wants to check if foreign goods are hurting its own factories, and it gives importers and exporters specific deadlines to submit evidence or request hearings.
analysis.analogy: It is like a local shopkeeper asking the local market committee to temporarily stop outsiders from selling cheap vegetables because it is destroying their own vegetable farm's business.
why_it_matters_india: Russia starts an official safeguard investigation into flat steel imports through its Department for Internal Market Defence.
Global steel trade rules under the World Trade Organization allow Russia to consider placing temporary restrictions on foreign steel if local harm is proven.
Global steel suppliers and metal markets react to potential trade barriers, which can alter where steel gets shipped around the world.
Indian steel makers and commodity prices feel the indirect ripples of shifts in global steel demand and trade flows.

impacts.target: Indian steel stocks like Tata Steel & JSW Steel
impacts.rationale: Changes in global trade barriers can alter export competition, which directly affects the business health and share prices of major steel producers — important for investors holding metal stocks.
If steel is blocked from entering Russia, it might get dumped into other global markets, lowering prices which can be good for buyers but tough for manufacturers.

watch_next: Whether Russia decides to impose actual import restrictions or tariffs after the investigation ends
Updates from the Eurasian Economic Union website regarding the flat steel safeguard case
analysis.caveats: This is a procedural WTO notification about an ongoing investigation, and Russia has not yet announced any final trade restrictions.

events.headline: Customs duty: India must reform its default payment process to minimize logistical delays

items.title: Customs duty: India must reform its default payment process to minimize logistical delays
items.summary: The country's customs regime must trust importers to collect cargo first and pay duty later as a default rule. Don’t hold shipments hostage—it slows business operations, constrains exports and makes it harder for India to join global value chains.

events.article_text:
Of the three great taxes India that collects, customs is an exception. Income arises today, tax on it is deposited monthly and returned annually. As for tax on consumption, a supply is made today, and goods can travel the country on an e-way bill without goods and services tax being paid, since GST is due only next month.

Import a consignment into India, however, and the goods will not be cleared until customs duty is paid. It could be the same taxpayer and the same government, but the country’s tax system operates on two opposite theories of trust, separated by a shoreline.

An exception to such stiff clearance already exists. Since 2016, under a facility drawn from the World Customs Organization, authorized economic operators (AEO) classified as tier 2 and above may clear their goods first—and revenue has not leaked. Trusted importers simply rotate the duty as working capital, like every other taxpayer with every other tax.

For such consignments, the release time at the country’s largest container port has fallen to about 41 hours in 2026, against roughly 77 hours for cargo that must pay before clearance. Yet, the club is microscopic. Only about 6,000 firms hold AEO status, mostly tier 1, which permits no deferral, while India has around 672,000 importers and exporters.

Those eligible to defer customs bills number about 1,500—well under 1%. And even where it exists, the facility is barely used: in 2026, it accounted for just 12% of bills of entry at seaports and 3% at land borders. A decade on, the overwhelming majority still pay duty before they get hold of shipments.

The facility follows the transaction, not the taxpayer. For instance, a tier-2 AEO firm with a bonded warehouse for manufacturing must still pay at the clearance point and cannot claim the deferral benefit. A facilitation available to a minuscule minority is not a policy. It is a privilege.

The objection to widening the facility out is that trust must be earned. But look at what AEO accreditation actually demands: on top of a compliance-and-solvency screening, a full supply-chain security audit—from premises and cargo integrity to infotech controls.

Yet, none of it is a measure of the odds that a firm will walk away from its duty. The better predictor of that is a company’s tax record, and the state already holds it: monthly GST returns, income tax filings, a compliance history scored in real-time.

An importer that files its GSTR-3B return every month is no stranger to the exchequer. Payment timing has no security implications; it is essentially a question of whether the state knows who owes it money. It always does.

The Union budget for 2026-27 took a welcome step with an Eligible Manufacturer Importer scheme that clears goods first and settles duty monthly; the Centre also widened the deferral window from 15 to 30 days for trusted importers.

The direction is right, but it is still hard for businesses to graduate to the AEO club, given the complexity of the process: a portal application, eligibility conditions, operational guidelines and a sunset clause that keeps it open till just March 2028. This easing does not reflect a substantial regime shift.

The cost of tight customs controls is measured at the berth. The finance ministry’s own National Time Release Studies identify the payment stage as a stubborn bottleneck. Importers scramble for immediate funds, manual banking interventions cascade after assessments, and all too often, the gains of advance filing and green channels dissipate at the last step because money must move before a container can.

Every hour that a cleared consignment waits for a paid challan is a toll taken on India’s attractiveness as a destination for investment and hub for global supply chains.

The fear of revenue leakage answers itself. Every importer holds an Import Export Code mapped to a GST identification number and a PAN number; every transaction is recorded. The Revised Kyoto Convention has urged for decades that the release of goods be separated from the final payment of duty. India signed up, but implementation has lagged.

The World Trade Organization Trade Facilitation Agreement that India ratified in 2016 obliges members to allow the release of goods before the final determination and payment of duty. The US, UK and EU already let compliant importers take delivery first and settle duty on a monthly cycle.

The treaty India signed and cargo-entry practices of its peers point one way. India, however, has confined it to a very thin band of AEO-certified traders, staying conservative.

A country whose ports release cargo early runs leaner supply chains: containers turn faster, detention and demurrage stop piling up, and congestion eases. In a world where businesses cannot afford any slack, time-release performance acts as an investment prospectus.

A reform that can improve that prospectus is to make deferred payments the statutory default for every registered importer. The regime should collect duty monthly, raise security issues only with a valid cause and deny access to shipments only for well recorded reasons. This will make a far bigger difference than a scheme that demands a portal application for inclusion in a closely vetted club.

India’s new customs law, whenever enacted, must collect customs duty the way India collects every other tax—after the goods have gone to work. A tax that in effect holds cargo hostage is a confession that the taxation system does not know its taxpayers. In 2026, with every importer mapped, measured and monitored in real-time, that’s no longer a sign of trade vigilance. It has long turned into a habit—and habits, unlike statutes, can and often need to be dropped for the better.

The authors are former officers, Indian Revenue Service.

analysis.tldr: If India allows businesses to pay import taxes later (like every other tax), goods will move faster through ports, making manufacturing cheaper and supply chains smoother.
the_story: Unlike income tax and GST (goods and services tax), which are paid after transactions happen, import customs duties must be paid upfront before goods are cleared.

A tiny group of trusted firms called authorized economic operators (AEO tier 2 and above) can clear goods first and pay later, reducing release time at India's largest container port to about 41 hours compared to 77 hours for others.
Only about 6,000 firms hold AEO status out of 672,000 importers and exporters, and fewer than 1% are eligible to defer customs bills.

The 2026-27 Union budget introduced an Eligible Manufacturer Importer scheme for monthly duty settlement and extended the deferral window from 15 to 30 days, but the process to qualify remains complex.
The article argues that India should make deferred monthly payments the default for all registered importers, aligning with global standards in the US, UK, EU, and WTO treaties.
analysis.what_happened: The article reports that India's current customs rules force importers to pay duty before releasing cargo, causing severe port delays. While a tiny group of trusted companies enjoys faster clearance and deferred payments, the vast majority must scramble for upfront cash, creating logistical bottlenecks at ports.
analysis.analogy: It is like a shopkeeper being forced to pay for wholesale goods upfront before walking out of the warehouse, whereas they normally pay their suppliers once a month after selling the items.
why_it_matters_india: Port congestion and container waiting times decrease because goods move out immediately instead of waiting for payment clearance steps.
Lower logistical friction reduces operational costs for manufacturing and importing companies across India.
Easier movement of raw materials boosts India's competitiveness as a global supply chain and manufacturing hub.
Faster turnaround times make India a more attractive destination for foreign investments.

impacts.target: Manufacturing sector margins (auto, electronics, heavy industry)
impacts.rationale: Lower port delays and better working capital management reduce costs for manufacturers relying on imported parts — good for companies and consumers.
Faster container clearance stops storage and penalty fees (demurrage) from piling up at ports — good for businesses.

watch_next: Updates on the implementation of the new customs law or broader rollout of deferred payment schemes
Changes to National Time Release Studies tracking port clearance times
analysis.caveats: The government may move slowly on broad reforms due to traditional fears of revenue leakage or tax evasion.

events.headline: Playing both sides of the U.S.-China AI “Cold War”

items.title: Playing both sides of the U.S.-China AI “Cold War”
items.summary: From Latin America to Southeast Asia, countries are dividing their AI investments between the two superpowers rather than choosing one over the other.

events.article_text:
Saudi Arabia celebrated the launch of what it calls the world’s most advanced Arabic-language AI model earlier this month. The technology behind it came from China even as the kingdom spends billions building its AI infrastructure with American companies.

The Arabic model, Humain-m3, is based on an open-source system from Chinese startup MiniMax. Humain, the state-backed company that commissioned the model, has struck major deals with Nvidia and other U.S. technology companies to build its AI computing capacity.

Saudi Arabia is not alone. From Latin America to Southeast and Central Asia, countries are buying American chips while adopting Chinese open-source models, splitting key AI projects between companies from two AI superpowers. The trend presents a growing complication for Washington’s competition with Beijing. Even countries investing heavily in American AI infrastructure are not necessarily choosing American technology for every layer of the AI stack.

“Many countries around the world, particularly in the Global South, want the best of both worlds,” Kyle Chan, a fellow at the John L. Thornton China Center at the Brookings Institution, told Rest of World. Many countries often do not attach the same security stigma to Chinese technology that Washington does, Chan said. “Ultimately, many countries around the world want to keep their options open and not be too dependent on any single source of technology.”

In August, Brazil announced an investment worth roughly $444 million into AI, which it effectively divided between Chinese and American technologies.

Around $255 million will go toward supercomputing infrastructure in Rio de Janeiro, developed in partnership with China’s HuaweiiHuaweiHuawei is a Chinese technology company focused on mobile phones and telecommunications, and is seen as a poster child for China’s global tech ambitions.READ MORE and iFlytek. The rest, around $189 million, will go to a separate supercomputer that Brazil is currently tendering, but expecting to source from Nvidia.

“The strategy is not to depend on a single company, technology or country,” President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s administration said in a statement, adding that the investments were intended to strengthen Brazil’s sovereignty over its data.

For most countries, technological sovereignty does not mean building an entire AI stack at home, Jesse Marks, a China-Middle East research scholar at the Australian National University, told Rest of World. Competing at the frontier has become prohibitively expensive, leaving governments to decide which technologies they can develop themselves and where they must rely on foreign suppliers.

For Saudi Arabia, it would be a “natural decision” to choose Chinese foundations for sovereign AI models if they perform better on relevant benchmarks, even if doing so carries political consequences with Washington, Marks said.

The U.S., however, has greater leverage in parts of the stack where its technology is harder to replace, such as advanced semiconductors, networking equipment, and sensitive cloud infrastructure. But Washington will struggle with countries that want AI but cannot afford American systems or software, Marks said.

“Outside of the network of American partners who are trusted or can afford it, it’s Chinese AI. It’s open models,” he said.

These technological choices are also becoming intertwined with countries’ broader diplomatic relationships. “AI is one of a number of portfolios that middle powers have to consider when negotiating with a partner like the United States,” Marks said.

Washington has accused Chinese labs of “free-riding” and training their models from frontier American AI models at an “industrial scale.” China, having rejected those accusations, has warned it would retaliate if Washington implements any curbs on Chinese AI companies.

Chinese companies are ramping up efforts to compete with American companies on different layers of the AI stack.

In Egypt, Huawei has bid to build AI data centers for the government, according to a source-based report by Bloomberg, competing against a proposal involving Nvidia. A successful bid would give Chinese companies another foothold in a market where AI infrastructure has so far been dominated by American technology.

Southeast Asia is another region where China-U.S. competition over technological influence is increasingly apparent.

Washington launched the U.S.-ASEAN AI Spark initiative in July, offering financial and technical support to Southeast Asian governments interested in adopting American AI technologies for public-sector use.

Malaysia is considering going in another direction, evaluating Huawei’s Ascend 910C accelerators as the backbone of its sovereign AI initiative, Bloomberg reported.

For now, the two AI superpowers appear to be taking different approaches to building influence abroad.

“China, like any leading power, wants the world to function in a manner that furthers its interests and replicates its own values,” Arindrajit Basu, a doctoral researcher in global governance of emerging technology at Leiden University, told Rest of World. “In the case of the internet and its allied technologies, this is a vision of governance providing a greater preference to the state in maintaining public order and security online. However, China is yet to engage in the naked coercion we have seen from the Trump administration that has reportedly clearly laid out an ultimatum.”

Washington is considering warning against countries trying to align with both U.S.- and China-led AI initiatives. That could put countries already engaging with both sides in a difficult position.

Kazakhstan, for example, has joined the U.S.-led Pax Silica initiative, which aims to build secure AI supply chains spanning semiconductors, compute, and other critical technologies. It has also joined China’s World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, or WAICO, which focuses on cooperation on AI developmen

analysis.tldr: Global AI rivalry could create mixed tech partnership opportunities and trade pressures for India as it navigates U.S. and Chinese tech ecosystems.
the_story: Saudi Arabia launched an advanced Arabic AI model called Humain-m3, using technology from Chinese startup MiniMax while simultaneously buying AI hardware from U.S. companies like Nvidia.

Experts note that many countries outside the West want to avoid depending on a single technology superpower and are mixing Chinese open-source AI with American hardware.

Broader global competition in AI infrastructure and open-source models could eventually lower software and computing costs, keeping consumer tech prices stable — good for household budgets.

history.title: The bubble that took thirty years to repay
history.what: At its 1989 peak the Tokyo stock market was worth more than the American one, and the land under the Imperial Palace was said to be worth more than all of California. The Nikkei then fell about 80% and did not regain its 1989 high until 2024 — thirty-five years later.
history.why: The 1985 Plaza Accord pushed the yen sharply higher, hurting exporters. The Bank of Japan cut rates hard to compensate, and the cheap money went into land and shares rather than into business investment. Banks lent against property using property as collateral, so rising prices justified more lending, which raised prices further. A closed loop, and everyone inside it could point to a rational-sounding reason.
history.impact: Households and banks spent two decades repairing balance sheets instead of spending and lending. Growth flatlined, prices actually fell for years, and a generation entered a frozen job market. Japan's share of world output fell from roughly 15% to under 5%.
history.policy: Rates went to zero and later below it. Japan invented quantitative easing in 2001 — a central bank creating money to buy government bonds — because conventional rate cuts had run out of room. Banks were eventually forced to recognise bad loans instead of rolling them over.
history.consequence: Every major central bank used Japan's playbook in 2008 and again in 2020, which is why zero rates and bond-buying stopped being exotic. Japan also proved an economy can stagnate for decades without a dramatic collapse — the danger is not always a crash.
history.pattern: When an asset is bought with debt secured against that same asset, the cycle feeds itself upward and then downward with equal force. Ask what the collateral is; if the collateral is the thing being bought, you are looking at the mechanism.
history.india_echo: Indian property lending and promoter share-pledging are the same shape on a smaller scale. It is why the RBI watches loan-to-value ratios, and why a promoter pledging shares to buy more shares deserves real suspicion.
history.watch_for: Lending growth running far ahead of income growth, with the asset itself as the security. That combination has never ended gently.
